item.title: A Neandertal-derived genetic variant reduces occipital brain volume in present-day humans.
item.description:
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
Neandertal crania were less globular than those of modern humans, suggesting differences in the relative volumes of brain regions, including the frontal and occipital lobes. Here, we show that a common genetic variant influencing occipital brain volume in present-day people was inherited from Neandertals. The variant lies in predicted transcription-factor recognition motifs near DAAM1, a gene that is known to be involved in brain development. Carriers of the Neandertal variant have altered DAAM1 expression and occipital lobe volumes that are about 0.85 cm³ smaller per gene copy. The variant is associated with reduced schizophrenia risk by almost 10% in homozygous carriers, while Neandertal ancestry as a whole does not show such a tendency. Any association with cognition or schooling is small or nonexistent, amounting to at most two weeks of education per allele against an average of about 15 y. Thus, this Neandertal-derived variant is linked to altered brain anatomy in present-day humans and lower schizophrenia risk while having little or no association with general cognitive ability.

item.title: Brain predictors of episodic memory change across race/ethnic groups: A machine learning investigation.
item.description:
Neuropsychology
OBJECTIVE: It is known that brain measures predict cognitive trajectories and that these predictions are not uniform across ethnoracial groups. But it remains unclear whether group differences reflect differing brain-cognition associations or similar associations but different demographic and brain health distributions. METHOD: We used eXtreme Gradient Boosting regression tree modeling to predict episodic memory (EM) trajectories from 64 brain measures, including regional gray matter thickness and white matter tract diffusion-tensor free water, with age, sex, education, and ethnoracial indicators in four well-established, ethnically and racially diverse U.S.-based cohorts. eXtreme Gradient Boosting combines many simple regression trees to model nonlinear relationships among predictors and outcome; predictor importance was ranked using SHapley Additive exPlanation values. RESULTS: In a sample of 1,463 participants (mean age, 77.0 ± 8.4 years; 503 African American, 168 Asian, 289 Hispanic, and 503 White), a computationally based gray matter signature and white matter tract hippocampal cingulum free-water brain measures ranked first and second in global importance to predict EM trajectory, followed by uncinate fasciculus free water. Generalized additive model analyses by ethnoracial group and age strata showed equivalent pairwise SHapley Additive exPlanation-brain dependency curves for the top two brain measures. Mean absolute deviations were less than 5% of between-participant standard deviation for EM slope, indicating that brain-outcome SHapley Additive exPlanation dependencies were similar across age and ethnoracial groups. CONCLUSION: EM trajectory prediction profiles reflect different sample compositions of brain health measures rather than different brain-EM associations. This suggests that observed variability in brain-EM predictors derives from group-specific distributions of demographic predictors and brain health. item.title: A hierarchical study of depression and subcortical gray matter volume in adults with HIV.
item.description:
Journal of neurovirology
Depression is highly prevalent in people with HIV (PWH). However, brain imaging studies of depression in PWH have been rather limited. We used a hierarchical approach to systematically investigate the impact of depression on subcortical volume in adults with HIV, focusing on the medial temporal lobe (MTL), the basal ganglia (BG), and the diencephalon. 99 PWH were included in the analysis (41-70 years old, 65% Black/African American, 25% female). Depression status was determined via the Beck Depression Inventory-II (BDI-II). Gray matter volume (GMv) of MTL, BG, diencephalon, and their subfields were estimated using FreeSurfer (v8.0.0). Linear regressions were performed in a hierarchical fashion to examine the association between depression and GMv of subcortical regions and subregions. The impacts of clinical and demographic factors were also examined. Depression was associated with lower GMv in the MTL (p = 0.014), but not the BG (p = 0.179) or diencephalon (p = 0.264). For subfields, depression was strongly associated with lower GMv in the hippocampal formation and most of its subfields, as well as in the basolateral and cortical-like regions and subnuclei of the amygdala. None of the viral factors were associated with any significant changes in GMv, including detectable viral load, nadir CD4, current CD4 count, and disease duration. In PWH, depression was associated with lower subcortical GMv, especially within the hippocampal formation and the basolateral amygdala, largely in accordance with the general population. Future longitudinal studies are needed to answer whether these associations continue or even grow throughout aging, and whether clinical factors play a role.

item.title: Spatial coupling between anosmia-related cortical alterations and regional gene expression: an imaging transcriptomics study.
item.description:
NeuroImage
The impact of anosmia on brain cortical structure and the underlying molecular mechanisms remain unclear. This study investigated causal associations between anosmia and cortical alterations using a multi-modal approach combining neuroimaging and genetics. High-resolution structural magnetic resonance imaging was acquired from 52 patients with anosmia and 50 healthy controls to extract cortical surface area (SA) and cortical thickness (TH). Mendelian randomization (MR) was employed to assess the causal effect of anosmia on cortical structure using summary statistics from the ENIGMA consortium. Furthermore, integrating gene expression data from the Allen Human Brain Atlas (AHBA), partial least squares regression (PLSR) and summary-data-based Mendelian randomization (SMR) were used to identify genes associated with changes in SA and TH due to anosmia. Gene enrichment analysis and cell type-specific analysis were then performed to explore the potential molecular mechanisms. Patients exhibited significantly reduced SA in the left rostral anterior cingulate and superior temporal sulcus, while TH was increased in regions including the left cuneus and supramarginal gyrus. MR analysis identified 11 cortical structural features nominally associated with anosmia, although none survived multiple comparison correction across 138 tests. Transcriptomic analysis identified genes correlated with these structural alterations, which were significantly enriched in synaptic pathways (e.g., postsynaptic membrane modulation) and specifically implicated GABAergic and glutamatergic neurons. Anosmia is causally associated with distinct cortical structural alterations. These regional changes are spatially coupled with molecular signatures involving synaptic function and neuronal plasticity, providing novel insights into the potential pathophysiology of olfactory loss.

item.title: Cortical Macro- and Microstructural Alterations in Multiple System Atrophy and Their Clinical Correlates.
item.description:
Movement disorders : official journal of the Movement Disorder Society
Multiple system atrophy (MSA) is primarily characterized by subcortical neurodegeneration. However, neuropathological evidence indicates that cortical neurodegeneration is also part of the disease. Conventional neuroimaging measures, such as cortical thickness (CTh), have been used to assess cortical macrostructural alterations, but findings remain limited and inconclusive. In this context, cortical mean diffusivity (cMD) has emerged as a promising marker of microstructural integrity, capturing alterations beyond macrostructural changes in other neurodegenerative disorders. However, its role in MSA remains largely unexplored. The objective of the study was to characterize cortical macro- and microstructural alterations in MSA and assess associations with clinical severity and cognitive performance. T1-weighted and diffusion magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), clinical, and neuropsychological assessments were obtained in 29 patients with MSA and 35 age- and sex-matched controls (HCs). Cortical macro- and microstructural alterations were evaluated using CTh and cMD, respectively. Group comparisons and correlations between MRI-derived cortical measures and clinical, cognitive, and neurodegeneration biomarkers were conducted (P < 0.05, false discovery rate [FDR]-corrected). Patients with MSA exhibited widespread increases in cMD, predominantly affecting the frontal and temporal cortices. This pattern partially overlapped with cortical thinning, although cMD alterations extended to rostral-lateral, rostral-medial, and inferior-medial regions. In MSA, increased cMD was associated with global cognitive impairment, whereas cortical thinning correlated with disease severity. MSA involves concurrent macro- and microstructural cortical alterations, with microstructural changes potentially preceding overt atrophy and indicating early pathology. Distinct cMD and CTh patterns suggest partially independent processes, whereas differential clinical associations highlight their complementarity. Together, these markers improve the characterization of cortical degeneration and disease heterogeneity. © 2026 The Author(s). item.title: Heterogeneous Negative Gray Matter Volume Deviations Converge on a Shared Depression Circuit Associated With Symptoms and rTMS Response.
item.description:
Advanced science (Weinheim, Baden-Wurttemberg, Germany)
Major depressive disorder (MDD) is characterized by marked heterogeneity in regional negative gray matter volume (GMV) deviations, obscuring the network basis of the disorder. Here, subject-specific normative GMV deviation maps are integrated with the human connectome using atrophy network mapping. Extreme negative GMV deviations in a medication-naive, first-episode MDD discovery cohort (n = 105) and an independent multisite validation cohort (n = 1265) converge on a reproducible depression circuit characterized by positive connectivity with subcortical-limbic regions and negative connectivity with frontoparietal and default mode network hubs. Circuit coupling tracks depressive symptom severity, follows gradients of depression-risk gene expression, and shows preliminary translational relevance: stronger negative connectivity at individualized rTMS targets is associated with greater clinical improvement. These findings reconcile heterogeneous structural deviations with the shared MDD phenotype and may inform future circuit-based neuromodulation studies.

item.title: Loneliness and the social brain: the mediating role of social functioning between nucleus accumbens structure and loneliness in aging.
item.description:
Social neuroscience
Loneliness is a complex and distressing emotional state linked to impaired health and well-being in later life. Although its behavioral and social correlates are well documented, the neural mechanisms underlying loneliness remain less clear. The nucleus accumbens (NAcc) plays a central role in reward processing and social motivation, suggesting its potential involvement in loneliness. The present study examined whether individual differences in loneliness are associated with structural variation in the NAcc, and whether social functioning mediates this relationship. Using high-resolution structural MRI in a sample of elderly participants, we measured NAcc volume and assessed loneliness alongside validated indices of social functioning. Results indicated that smaller NAcc volume was significantly related to higher loneliness, and this association was statistically consistent with an indirect effect via reduced social functioning. These findings highlight the neural underpinnings of loneliness in aging and underscore the importance of social functioning as a pathway linking brain structure to subjective social experience.

item.title: The impaired white matter integrity and altered functional connectivity in Parkinson's disease.
item.description:
Magnetic resonance imaging
Purpose Parkinson's disease (PD) is a neurodegenerative disorder characterized by structural abnormalities in the cerebral cortex and subcortical regions. Nevertheless, functional connectivity (FC) alterations within these affected white matter (WM) regions have not been fully clarified. Methods We combine diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) and resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI) to explore abnormalities in WM structure and FC in 20 PD patients and 22 age- and gender-matched healthy controls (HCs). Results Compared with the HCs, PD patients showed lower fractional anisotropy (FA) values in multiple widespread WM tracts, including the the forceps minor, the bilateral inferior longitudinal fasciculus, the right inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus, corticospinal tract (CST) and superior longitudinal fasciculus (SLF), the left anterior thalamic radiation (ATR), uncinate fasciculus and cingulum. Seed-based FC analysis revealed that: for the CST seed, PD patients exhibited reduced FC with the bilateral postcentral gyrus and precentral gyrus, the right superior occipital gyrus and left inferior parietal lobule. For the SLF seed, PD patients exhibited reduced FC with the bilateral anterior cingulate cortex. For the ATR seed, hypoconnectivity was found in multiple cerebellar subregions, including the bilateral cerebellum VIII and cerebellum IX, the right cerebellum VI and cerebellar crus I, and the left middle temporal gyrus. Conclusion Our findings indicate that PD patients exhibit widespread WM microstructural damage and some of these damaged fibers show abnormal FC, which may account for motor deficits and cognitive decline observed in PD. The combined use of DTI and rs-fMRI provides novel perspectives on the neural mechanisms underlying PD.

item.title: Longitudinal association between baseline brain entropy and gray matter volume changes in Shidu parents: A five-year multimodal MRI study.
item.description:
Journal of affective disorders
Background People who have lost their only child (Shidu parents) may experience prolonged bereavement-related psychological trauma. Although structural brain alterations have been reported, whether baseline functional complexity is associated with subsequent gray matter volume (GMV) changes remains unclear. Methods This study included 66 Shidu parents and 33 healthy controls. Five-year longitudinal structural MRI was used to assess GMV changes in Shidu parents, and baseline brain entropy (BEN) was derived from resting-state fMRI. Linear mixed-effects models identified regions with significant GMV changes. We then examined associations between baseline BEN and the annualized percent change in GMV (GMV-APC) within these regions, the incremental explanatory value of BEN, and whether these associations differed by GMV change direction. Results During the five-year follow-up, 35 brain regions showed significant GMV changes within the Shidu parent group, including GMV decreases in 27 regions and GMV increases in 8 regions. Further analyses showed that baseline BEN was significantly associated with GMV-APC in 6 regions showing GMV decreases and 2 regions showing GMV increases. Overall, these associations were predominantly observed in regions showing GMV decreases, and baseline BEN provided additional explanatory information related to subsequent GMV changes beyond that explained by baseline GMV. Conclusion A five-year longitudinal follow-up showed that baseline BEN was associated with subsequent GMV changes, providing neuroimaging evidence for the relationship between brain functional complexity and gray matter structural changes in the context of long-term trauma associated with the loss of an only child.

item.title: Associations between white matter network alterations and visuospatial and social-emotional deficits in patients with right hemisphere tumors: a prospective clinico-radiological study.
item.description:
Brain structure & function
Preserving neurological function is crucial in brain tumor surgery. Because the right hemisphere supports visuospatial and social‑cognitive abilities, damage may affect quality of life. This prospective study (TANGO; ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT04288505) examined associations between visuospatial and social‑emotional deficits and tractography‑based white matter alterations in patients with right hemisphere tumors. Thirty‑four patients were assessed preoperatively and 22 postoperatively using diffusion magnetic resonance imaging and four neuropsychological tests. Tractography metrics were extracted for nine right hemisphere tracts. Thirty‑four Human Connectome Project participants served as controls. Preoperatively, deficits in visuospatial functioning, facial emotion recognition, and mentalizing were associated with predominantly right hemisphere microstructural abnormalities within distributed white matter networks. Visuospatial deficits were associated with alterations involving the frontal aslant tract (FAT), arcuate fasciculus (AF), superior longitudinal fasciculus (SLF), and SLF II; facial emotion recognition deficits with the SLF III and uncinate fasciculus (UF); and mentalizing deficits with the AF. Postoperatively, exploratory findings suggested associations between new social-emotional deficits and structural alterations involving the inferior longitudinal fasciculus (ILF), SLF, and SLF III, whereas new visuospatial deficits showed a trend toward reduced right FAT volume. Relative to controls, left hemisphere tractographic changes were observed regardless of the presence of visuospatial and/or social-emotional deficits, whereas right hemisphere alterations were primarily observed in patients with such deficits. These findings highlight the role of right hemisphere networks in supporting visuospatial and social-emotional functioning. Further characterization of white matter connectivity may help improve risk stratification, surgical planning, and rehabilitation strategies.

item.title: T1 contrast at the gray-white matter boundary during adolescence and its associations with cortical thickness and gyrification.
item.description:
Brain structure & function
The advent of surface-based morphometry has facilitated the detailed evaluation of cortical features such as thickness and folding. However, developmental and clinical studies yield inconsistent findings across these cortical indices, partly due to biological and methodological factors that contribute to their estimation. Using T1-weighted images from over 500 healthy participants in the Philadelphia Neurodevelopmental Cohort (PNC), we investigated age-related differences in T1 contrast at the gray-white matter boundary (T1 contrast) during adolescence and assessed its impact on the estimation of the age-related differences of cortical thickness and local gyrification index. T1 contrast showed a significant positive correlation with age. With increasing age, cortical thickness exhibited a linear decline, whereas local gyrification index exhibited a quadratic decline. Controlling for T1 contrast attenuated the associations between age and both cortical indices. Furthermore, white matter volume was significantly associated not only with T1 contrast but also with cortical thickness and local gyrification index. Nevertheless, age-related associations of both cortical indices remained significant after accounting for T1 contrast. These findings highlight the importance of accounting for T1 contrast when interpreting age-related differences in cortical measures in developmental neuroimaging research.

item.title: Fixel-based analysis identifies selective vulnerability of non-dominant fiber populations in aging and mild cognitive impairment.
item.description:
Brain structure & function
Fixel-based analysis (FBA) resolves fiber-specific white matter properties within crossing-fiber regions, where conventional diffusion tensor imaging is limited. We applied single-shell three-tissue constrained spherical deconvolution to diffusion MRI from 295 older adults in the Vanderbilt Memory and Aging Project cohort, quantifying fiber density (FD), fiber-bundle cross-section (FC), and their composite (FDC) across the primary (N1), secondary (N2), and tertiary (N3) fiber populations within each white matter voxel. White matter was stratified into crossing-fiber complexity strata defined by the number of distinct bundles per voxel, and covariate-adjusted models examined associations with age, cognitive status, and cognition. FC declined with age most steeply in the non-dominant fiber populations. In these populations, FC was lower in participants with mild cognitive impairment than in cognitively unimpaired participants, and higher FC was associated with better executive function. The age-related decline in non-dominant FC did not vary across crossing-fiber complexity, indicating that fiber-population identity, rather than local architecture, organizes age-related vulnerability. FD and FDC showed age associations that became more positive as complexity increased, with the N1 FD association reversing from negative in the least complex regions to positive in the most complex. This behavior is consistent with how density is estimated in multi-fiber voxels rather than with fiber loss, identifying FC as the more interpretable metric in crossing-fiber regions. These findings identify fiber cross-section in the non-dominant fiber populations as a sensitive marker of white matter aging and cognitive status and provide a framework for fiber-specific analysis in existing single-shell cohorts.

item.title: Probabilistic mapping of brain connections without random sampling
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
For two decades, most tractography has mapped brain connections by sampling millions of pathways probabilistically. Sampling makes results non-deterministic and costly to store. We show that it is unnecessary: modeling tractography as an absorbing Markov chain gives the expected result of infinitely many streamlines. This approach is more reliable than streamline-based tractography across test--retest scans. It readily maps tracts in clinical-grade data and neonates, around tumors and along small pathways. MPAT is available as open-source software at https://github.com/rokemlab/mpat .

item.title: State-dependent structure-function coupling reflects dynamic engagement of the brain's structural scaffold
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Functional brain organization is shaped by the brain's anatomical scaffold, yet how structure-function coupling varies across cognitive states remains unclear. Across 723 adults from two independent cohorts, we examined coupling using diffusion and functional magnetic resonance imaging. In the primary cohort, coupling was strongest during movie-watching, intermediate during rest, and weakest during working memory, declining further with increasing working-memory load. The movie-rest difference replicated in an independent sample, challenging the primacy of rest for revealing anatomical constraints. State effects were superimposed on a stable unimodal-to-transmodal cortical hierarchy, with movie-watching preferentially enhancing coupling in sensory and language systems. Regions with more stable functional connectivity across states showed stronger coupling. Older age was associated with lower auditory and somatomotor coupling in both cohorts, alongside heterogeneous increases in association cortex. Together, we show that cognitive context shapes structure-function alignment, supporting a framework of complementary structure-constrained and distributed-integrative modes of communication.

item.title: Non-invasive temporal interference stimulation targeting the hippocampus enhances fast motor memory consolidation
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Converging neuroimaging evidence indicates that the hippocampus is involved in motor sequence learning (MSL) and its consolidation at multiple timescales. However, direct evidence for a causal role of the hippocampus in these processes in healthy humans remains scarce, partly due to the inability of conventional non-invasive brain stimulation techniques to reach this deep brain structure. Here, we used temporal interference stimulation (TIS) - a technique enabling non-invasive stimulation targeted toward deep brain regions - to probe the functional role of the hippocampus in MSL and its consolidation. In two separate experiments, sixty-four young healthy adults (36 females) received, in within-subject counterbalanced designs, active (5 Hz envelope) or control (0 Hz envelope) hippocampal-targeted TIS either during active practice of an MSL task (task-TIS experiment, n = 32) or during the short rest periods interleaved with task practice known to support rapid forms of consolidation (rest-TIS experiment, n = 32). Consolidation was assessed at both the micro timescale (i.e., over the short "micro-offline" rest intervals interspersed with task practice) and macro timescale (i.e., over a 24-hour "macro-offline" retention interval). Our results indicate that TIS targeting the hippocampus during inter-practice rest periods - but not during task practice - significantly enhanced micro-offline gains in performance as compared to control stimulation. While this effect did not carry over to the 24-hour retention interval at the group level, participants with greater stimulation-induced micro-offline gains showed larger overnight performance improvements. These findings provide the first direct evidence that experimental interventions targeting the hippocampus modulate offline motor memory consolidation processes.

item.title: Middle Temporal Gyrus Neurite Microstructure and Scam Susceptibility in Older Adults Without Dementia
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
Background: Financial exploitation is a prevalent public health concern among older adults, and emerging evidence links vulnerability to gray matter macrostructure and white matter microstructure, including within brain regions and networks implicated in early Alzheimer's disease. Although diffusion tensor imaging is sensitive to age-related variation in brain microstructure, its scalar metrics cannot distinguish among the tissue properties contributing to observed differences. Neurite orientation dispersion and density imaging (NODDI) models distinct tissue compartments, yielding estimates of neurite density, dendritic complexity, and extracellular free water. Methods: This study examined associations between scam susceptibility and NODDI metrics using ultra-high-field 7-Tesla imaging in 116 older adults without dementia. Neurite density index (NDI), orientation dispersion index (ODI), and free-water fraction were quantified within seven a priori regions of interest linked to early Alzheimer's disease. Multivariate regressions evaluated associations between scam susceptibility and NODDI metrics, adjusting for age, sex, education, and global cognition, with multiple comparison correction within each metric. For significant regions, post-hoc hierarchical regression models tested whether NODDI metrics explained variance beyond regional cortical thickness, total gray matter, and total intracranial volume. Results: Greater scam susceptibility was associated with higher NDI (β=0.30, pFDR=.025) and lower ODI (β=-0.28, pFDR=.044) in the middle temporal gyrus (MTG). No other regions survived correction. Additionally, MTG NDI and ODI explained variance beyond macrostructure measures. Conclusions: These findings identify NODDI metrics as novel microstructural correlates of scam susceptibility beyond macrostructure, supporting investigation of their relevance to financial vulnerability in older age.

item.title: Denoised gray matter BOLD-CSF coupling in aging and its association with markers of preclinical AD
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Global gray matter (gGM) blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) signal fluctuations are temporally coupled with cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) inflow. Reduced gGM BOLD-CSF coupling has been reported in aging and linked to Alzheimer’s disease (AD)-related pathology. Our study aimed to investigate the effect of multi-echo denoising on age-related reductions in coupling and whether coupling is associated with cortical thickness across AD-vulnerable regions and crystallized–fluid ability (‘CF’) discrepancy, markers of preclinical AD. We analyzed an open-access behavioral/MRI dataset (n = 301) cognitively healthy younger and older adults (OpenNeuro ds003592). Coupling scores were calculated as correlations between gGM signal fluctuations and CSF inflow signals, before and after denoising. Linear mixed models tested the effects of age and denoising on coupling, while multiple regression models assessed associations between denoised coupling, cortical thickness, and CFdiscrepancy. Coupling was lower in older versus younger adults. Denoising significantly reduced coupling in younger adults but not in older adults. Both gGM and CSF signal amplitudes were lower in older adults. Denoised coupling was not significantly associated with cortical thickness or CFdiscrepancy, and cortical thickness was not associated with CFdiscrepancy after controlling for age. These findings support age-related differences in BOLD–CSF coupling, which itself may not be related to coarse markers of preclinical AD.

item.title: Age-related processes impacting cognitive processing speed across an older adult cohort: A drift diffusion model analysis.
item.description:
PloS one
The time we take to perform a cognitive task increases with age, which is a principal contributor to cognitive aging. The drift diffusion model is widely applied to decompose processes that may contribute to age-related slowing, with the drift rate parameter reflecting the rate of information accumulation until a decision is made. This age-related slowing is hypothesized to relate to changes in cerebral white matter microstructure. Our aim in this preregistered study (https://osf.io/yhn4m) was to evaluate the cross-sectional age-related differences in processes underlying age-related slowing across an older adult cohort and explore the role of white matter change in such age-related slowing. We found age to be associated with drift rate in an emotion recognition and a memory task but not in a delay discounting task; in an exploratory analysis, an indirect association involving global fractional anisotropy was observed for the emotion recognition task, although this did not survive multiple-comparison correction. Our results suggest age-related differences in information processing across cognitive contexts, although formal comparisons between tasks were not conducted. A fuller understanding of the mechanisms of cognitive slowing with age will help tailor intervention strategies and could inform environmental modifications promoting older adults' functional independence and quality of life.

item.title: The aging human brain exhibits reduced hemodynamic and cerebrospinal fluid flow waves during sleep.
item.description:
Nature aging
Aging reduces the quality and quantity of sleep, and sleep disruption is predictive of neurodegeneration and cognitive decline. Sleep loss could affect brain health through disruption of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) circulation, which is important for brain homeostasis. In young adults, large CSF flow waves appear during non-rapid eye movement sleep; however, whether sleep-dependent brain fluid physiology changes in aging is not known. Here we imaged large-scale CSF flow and hemodynamics in young (18-39 years) and older (60-84 years) adults during nighttime sleep. Sleep-dependent CSF flow was reduced in older adults, and was linked to reduced EEG slow wave power, decreased global hemodynamic oscillations and gray matter atrophy. Using sensory and vasoactive stimuli to drive CSF flow, we found that both neural and cerebrovascular changes contributed to this disruption. These results demonstrate reduced CSF flow during sleep in human aging, before disease onset, and identify parallel neural and hemodynamic mechanisms contributing to this decline.

item.title: The many facets of human brain asymmetry.
item.description:
Nature reviews. Neuroscience
Asymmetry on the left-right axis is an organizing principle of the human brain that is important for diverse cognitive and behavioural functions. Advances in neuroimage analysis, genomics and large-scale data collection in the past decade have transformed our understanding of the biological foundations and multivariate nature of brain asymmetry. In this Review, we synthesize evidence across scales - from functional and macro-anatomical asymmetries and their inter-relations to microstructural, cellular and molecular levels. We examine inter-individual variation and atypical forms of brain asymmetry, which reveal that diverse aspects of asymmetry can vary largely independently across individuals rather than constituting a single trait. In this context, we discuss the developmental origins, lifespan trajectories and genetic architecture of hemispheric differences. We also summarize the relevance of brain asymmetry for neurological and psychiatric disorders and evolutionary changes of brain asymmetry that occurred in humans. Through this synthesis, we illustrate how contrasting the left and right hemispheres provides an informative window into the multi-level brain organization that supports cognition and behaviour.

item.title: Mesoscale connectivity of substructures within the human amygdaloid complex.
item.description:
NeuroImage
The amygdala operates as an integrative network hub, participating in emotional, cognitive, and distributed neural circuit functions. Though once thought of as a single anatomical entity, the amygdala is increasingly being recognized as a complex network of functionally and anatomically distinct nuclei and substructures. Mesoscale diffusion MR images (250 μm isotropic acquisition, upsampled to 125 μm) of the post-mortem human temporal lobe were acquired to allow the identification of the structural components of the amygdaloid complex, which includes the amygdala, as well as the surrounding transitional areas. Amygdala nuclei, including their 13 subnuclei and related substructures were defined, delineated and segmented to generate a unique 3-dimensional visualization of the amygdaloid complex in its anatomical context. Volumetric analyses and scalar indices revealed its morphological and microstructural composition, whereas tractography exposed the intra-amygdala connectome. Both canonical and non-canonical pathways were identified and quantified for a more in-depth network analysis. A virtual dissection of pathways involving the lateral nucleus, which is the largest nucleus (33% of the amygdala), for instance, showed numerous extra-amygdala pathways, as well as intra-amygdala pathways, consistent with its well-established role as the primary input site to the amygdala. A majority of connections are localized in the dorsal lateral subnucleus, which can be conceived of as the dominant gateway for afferent integration. In contrast, the central nucleus, emerged as the primary output hub from the amygdala. This intra-amygdala connectome framework establishes a structural roadmap that advances a mechanistic understanding and informs future network-based therapeutic strategies for neurological and psychiatric disorders.

item.title: Altered individual-level morphological similarity brain networks in late-life subthreshold depression: Preserved global topology with selective nodal and sub-network disruptions.
item.description:
International psychogeriatrics
Objectives Subthreshold depression (StD) is prevalent in older adults and increases the risk of major depressive disorder, but its large-scale brain-network organization remains poorly understood. Individual-level morphological similarity networks estimate interregional structural covariance separately for each participant. Methods 110 older women (56 StD, 54 comparison participants) underwent T1-weighted MRI. Individual networks were constructed using Jensen-Shannon divergence-based similarity (JSDs) between gray matter volume distributions across 116 AAL regions. Graph metrics were assessed across sparsity 0.05-0.40 with Benjamini-Hochberg false-discovery-rate (FDR) control, and the network-based statistic identified altered sub-networks (5000 permutations, FWE-corrected). Reproducibility was tested with an alternative Kullback-Leibler metric (KLDs) and 4-mm smoothing. Results Both groups showed preserved small-world global topology. Participants with StD had increased left hippocampal degree centrality (p = 0.0013), reduced nodal efficiency in the right inferior occipital (p = 0.0046) and right postcentral gyri (p = 0.0085), and a 50-node, 73-edge hypoconnectivity sub-network (pFWE = 0.0408); none of these regional findings survived FDR correction. Right inferior occipital efficiency was inversely associated with reminiscence and rumination, and right postcentral efficiency positively with cognition and extraversion. The hippocampal finding was reproduced using KLDs (p = 0.0012) and 4-mm smoothing (p = 0.0049). In 74 patients with major depressive disorder, global topology was likewise preserved but without corresponding nodal alterations. Conclusions Late-life StD shows preserved global topology with focal nodal and sub-network disruptions. Hippocampal hyper-connectivity may reflect compensatory reorganization, whereas occipitotemporal and somatosensory hypoconnectivity is associated with reminiscence, rumination and cognitive function. Individual-level networks may provide a sensitive framework for characterising subclinical network alterations, pending confirmation in larger samples.

item.title: Whole-brain white matter fractional anisotropy across baseball expertise levels: a TBSS study.
item.description:
Brain structure & function
While sports-related sensorimotor experience has been associated with differences in brain structure and function, evidence regarding white matter (WM) microstructural differences in high-speed open-skilled sports remains limited. Prior studies have often been constrained by small sample sizes or analyses restricted to selected tracts. To address these limitations, this study employed voxel-wise tract-based spatial statistics (TBSS) to examine whole-brain fractional anisotropy (FA) in 142 participants: 50 highly skilled baseball (SB) players, 45 intermediate baseball (IB) players, and 47 non-player (NP) controls. TBSS revealed that the SB group exhibited significantly higher FA than the IB and/or NP groups across multiple projection and cerebellar pathways, including the pontine crossing tract, corona radiata, posterior limb of the internal capsule, superior cerebellar peduncle, and cerebral peduncle, as well as association pathways (superior fronto-occipital fasciculus and sagittal stratum), commissural pathways (corpus callosum and tapetum), and the fornix (crus)/stria terminalis. Follow-up ROI analyses showed significant group effects in seven of 16 selected tracts, including the pontine crossing tract, body of the corpus callosum, left superior corona radiata, bilateral posterior corona radiata, and bilateral tapetum. Across these tracts, the SB group consistently demonstrated higher FA than the IB and/or NP groups. Together, these results indicate that FA differences across expertise levels were primarily characterized by higher values in skilled players rather than a uniform increase across the three groups. item.title: Microstructural alterations of human medial temporal lobe in dementia: volumetric and DTI findings correlate with cell number and neuropathology.
item.description:
Brain structure & function
Volumetric and diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) alterations in medial temporal lobe (MTL) regions are consistently reported in Alzheimer's disease (AD). However, their biological basis remains poorly understood. We combined Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) metrics with cellular quantification and neuropathological burden assessment to investigate microstructural substrates underlying MTL imaging alterations in human donors with known cognitive and neuropathological status. Absolute cell numbers were quantified in a cohort of 54 brain donors using the isotropic fractionator, and postmortem MRI was performed on a subset of 18 fixed brain hemispheres. To assess microstructural brain alterations associated with disease progression, in vivo volumetric and DTI metrics were analyzed in 39 cognitively unimpaired controls (CU), 31 individuals with mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and 14 patients with clinical AD dementia. In the postmortem cohort, MTL diffusivity metrics showed moderate negative correlations with total cell numbers. Mean, axial, and radial diffusivity positively correlated with Braak stage, whereas fractional anisotropy (FA) correlated negatively with CERAD score, linking diffusion alterations to AD-related pathology. In vivo MTL analyses revealed increased mean, axial, and radial diffusivity, and reduced FA in AD patients compared with both CU and MCI individuals. The MCI group exhibited intermediate alterations in diffusivity. Differences between in vivo and postmortem diffusion values were consistent with tissue fixation, temperature, and variations in acquisition protocols. Our findings suggest that diffusion MRI alterations in the MTL are associated with reduced cellularity and neuropathological burden, supporting the biological relevance of DTI metrics as markers of microstructural degeneration in AD.

item.title: MRI Microscopic Fractional Anisotropy Differences in Genetic Frontotemporal Degeneration.
item.description:
Journal of magnetic resonance imaging : JMRI
Background In genetic frontotemporal degeneration (FTD), cortical and subcortical brain volume differences have been detected using volumetric MRI decades before symptoms appear. Microscopic fractional anisotropy (μFA) is a diffusion MRI metric that is sensitive to diffusion anisotropy regardless of relative fiber orientations within a voxel and is more accurate than conventional DTI metrics for detecting age-related microstructural changes in healthy individuals and differences in some neurological diseases. Purpose To compare μFA, mean diffusivity (MD), and volume between genetic frontotemporal degeneration (FTD) variant carriers and non-carriers in the insula, frontal pole, and medial orbitofrontal cortex. Study type Cross-sectional cohort study. Population Carriers of FTD variants in C9orf72, GRN, or MAPT (n = 12; age = 56.7 ± 8.12 years; 50% female) and familial non-variant carriers (n = 8; age = 59.5 ± 10.3 years; 62.5% female). Field strength/sequence 3T; Magnetization prepared rapid acquisition with gradient echoes (MPRAGE) sequence (anatomical imaging) and a diffusion echo-planar imaging sequence with modified diffusion gradients for spherical tensor encoding (μFA measurement). Assessment MPRAGE images underwent cortical and subcortical segmentation to obtain regions of interest. MD and μFA maps were derived from diffusion MRI data. μFA, MD, and volumes were compared between FTD variant carriers (n = 5 symptomatic, and n = 7 asymptomatic) and familial non-carriers. Statistical tests Linear models with heteroscedasticity-consistent confidence intervals were computed to analyze between-group differences in outcomes while controlling for age (alpha = 0.05). Results FTD variant carriers exhibited significantly lower insula μFA than non-carriers (η2 p = 0.22). Post hoc contrasts showed significantly reduced insula μFA in symptomatic carriers compared to non-carriers (d = 1.57). Mean μFA in asymptomatic carriers (mean ± standard error (SE): 0.454 ± 0.010) was not significantly different to that in non-carriers (mean ± SE: 0.471 ± 0.009, p = 0.465), nor in symptomatic carriers (mean ± SE: 0.430 ± 0.012, p = 0.290). Data conclusion μFA is reduced in the insula, a region vulnerable to early atrophy in FTD, reflecting microstructural changes in genetic FTD with greater effect sizes than MD and volume. Evidence level 2. Technical efficacy Stage 2.

item.title: DECODE: DEcomposition of COupled and DEcoupled Brain States: Separating Structure-Coupled and Structure-Decoupled Functional Organization in Alzheimers Disease
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Brain functional activity emerges within an underlying structural scaffold. While structural network connectivity provides a relatively stable anatomical backbone for large-scale communication, functional interactions are high-dimensional and temporally dynamic, forming recurrent patterns that can be represented in a latent space of transient functional states. Yet, how these transient functional states are organized and the extent to which they remain constrained by structural network connectivity or become relatively decoupled from structural organization over time remain poorly understood. To address this gap, we introduce DECODE (DEcomposition of COupled and DEcoupled Brain States), a data-driven latent-space framework that uses independent component analysis (ICA) and multimodal data to decompose resting-state dynamic functional network connectivity into a lower-dimensional representation of transient functional states. These states capture temporally varying structure-coupled and structure-decoupled patterns using diffusion MRI-derived structural network connectivity priors. Structure-coupled states reflect functional configurations more strongly anchored to major structural motifs, whereas structure-decoupled states represent configurations less constrained by the identified structural organization, while potentially remaining within structurally defined dynamical bounds. DECODE identifies reproducible structure-coupled and structure-decoupled states, with mean squared error reconstruction of dynamic information < 0.1 and adjusted R-squared = 0.4. Applied to Alzheimers disease (AD), DECODE revealed stronger group differences (FDR-corrected p-value 0.05) in both connectivity organization and temporal dynamics for decoupled states. These findings suggest that functional states less constrained by identified structural organization may be more vulnerable to AD-related disruption, whereas structure-coupled states may be relatively preserved. More broadly, DECODE provides a reproducible and generalizable framework for quantifying how functional dynamics are shaped by, or diverge from, structural organization by incorporating a latent representation of the structural connectome as an informative prior. Our findings established structural and functional alignment variation by distinguishing dynamic functional patterns closely coupled with structure from those that deviate from it.

item.title: Environmental Exposures and Brain Magnetic Resonance Imaging Phenotypes in Cognitively Healthy Ageing: A Systematic Review
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
Background: Air pollution and built environment features are increasingly associated with negative health outcomes, yet their relation to brain health in cognitively healthy older adults remains unclear. Methods: To synthesise the extant literature, we conducted a systematic review, searching MEDLINE (PubMed) and Web of Science (Core Collection) from inception to February 23, 2026. Eligible studies assessed a natural or built environmental exposure against brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) measures in cognitively healthy older adults (ages 65+). Reviewers screened and extracted summary data from published reports in Covidence; no individual patient data were sought. The main outcome was brain health; findings were synthesised narratively using an effect-direction approach, as heterogeneous exposures, outcomes, and effect metrics precluded pooling. Findings: Of 2,496 records screened, 27 studies met eligibility, comprising >84,000 older adults across 10 countries: United States, South Korea, United Kingdom, France, Spain, Sweden, Netherlands, Taiwan, Germany, and Japan. Thirteen studies were cross-sectional and 14 were cohort studies (nine observational and five longitudinal). Higher air pollution exposure—particularly PM2.5, NO2, and PM10—was associated with altered brain structure: smaller total, grey matter, and white matter volumes, greater white matter hyperintensities, cortical thinning, and smaller medial temporal and hippocampal volumes; greenspace was associated with more favourable brain structure in several mostly cross-sectional studies, though findings were not uniform. Thirteen studies met criteria for high methodological quality and low though not uniform risk of bias; outcome assessment was a recurring source of bias (12 of 27 studies), and four of the five longitudinal studies did not meet criterion for follow-up adequacy.Interpretation: This review synthesises emerging observational evidence that air pollution is associated with differences in brain structure in cognitively healthy ageing. Because the included evidence is predominantly cross-sectional, these associations are hypothesis generating; if confirmed in longitudinal studies, this modifiable exposure could serve as a potential target for policymakers aiming to protect brain health in the fastest growing segment of the global population.

item.title: A realistic model of resting-state BOLD spectra in white matter
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Resting-state BOLD signals in white matter show a spectral elevation near 0.06 Hz on an exponentially decaying background, and white-matter hemodynamic response functions (HRFs) have a prominent initial dip. We model the resting signal as shot noise: randomly timed neural events are filtered by the HRF, so that the spectrum is the input spectrum multiplied by the squared HRF gain, plus instrumental noise. The initial dip and post-stimulus undershoot remove low-frequency power, making the white-matter HRF a band-pass filter with maximum gain near 0.05 Hz. One set of physiological parameters fits both a measured white-matter HRF (R² = 0.993) and the group-mean white-matter spectrum (R² = 0.987), with a resting transit time of about 4 s and a metabolic response weighted about twice as heavily as in gray matter. Deepening the dip raises the filter gain and moves its maximum toward 0.06 Hz, linking the dip to the spectral feature. A narrower line in individual spectra is reproduced either by an underdamped HRF that matches the measured response over its first 20 s or by a rhythmic input near 0.06 Hz. The model identifies which HRF properties could explain the decline of the peak with age.

item.title: Opposite Modulations of Thalamo-Cingulate and Fronto-IFOF Gray-White Matter Circuits Underlie Symptomatic and Cognitive Gains with Magnetic Seizure Therapy in Schizophrenia
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Magnetic seizure therapy (MST) has shown promise for treating schizophrenia, but the functional brain changes associated with its clinical and cognitive outcomes remain unclear. We investigated gray matter–white matter (GM–WM) functional connectivity and its associations with symptom and cognitive changes following MST. Fifty-three patients with schizophrenia and 40 demographically matched healthy controls underwent baseline resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging; 33 patients with usable pretreatment and post-treatment imaging data were included in longitudinal analyses. Functional connectivity was compared between groups and across treatment time points, and connectivity changes were examined in relation to clinical and cognitive changes. Following MST, patients showed reductions in psychotic symptoms and improvements in the MATRICS Consensus Cognitive Battery composite score and processing speed. Treatment-related connectivity changes predominantly involved GM–WM connections. Decreased connectivity within a thalamus–corona radiata–cingulate circuit was associated with symptom improvement, whereas increased connectivity involving the left inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus and frontal regions was associated with cognitive improvement. Exploratory atlas-based analyses identified spatial associations between functional connectivity patterns and normative histaminergic and serotonergic receptor distributions, including 5-HT4 receptor maps. These findings suggest that symptom and cognitive improvements following MST are associated with changes in GM–WM functional connectivity. The receptor mapping results provide an exploratory neurochemical context for these associations, rather than evidence of treatment-induced changes in neurotransmitter levels or receptor availability.

item.title: Beyond sleep macrostructure: a high-definition review of acupuncture's electrophysiological signatures in modulating sleep microarchitecture (spectral power, spindles, and slow oscillations).
item.description:
Brain structure & function
Sleep science has shifted from coarse stage-based metrics toward a microstructural perspective that treats electroencephalographic biomarkers, spectral power, sleep spindles, and slow oscillations as candidate windows onto restorative brain function. This high-definition review evaluates whether acupuncture has been shown to modify these features. Direct evidence from natural overnight sleep is currently very limited: most available electrophysiological studies were conducted during quiet wakefulness, in resting daytime EEG recordings from clinical groups, or under propofol anesthesia. These studies demonstrate that acupuncture or related electrical acupoint stimulation can produce state-, region-, and frequency-dependent changes in EEG power and network organization, but they do not yet establish increased NREM spindle density, improved slow-oscillation-spindle coupling, enhanced slow-wave morphology, memory consolidation, or glymphatic clearance. We therefore distinguish directly observed findings from indirect mechanistic support and from hypotheses that require prospective testing. Plausible pathways include ascending somatosensory influences on thalamocortical excitability, autonomic and hypothalamic effects that may reduce hyperarousal, and peripheral or central neurochemical processes involving adenosine, GABA, serotonin, and BDNF; however, the causal sequence from needling to sleep microarchitecture remains unproven. Future progress requires preregistered, adequately powered, multi-night studies using validated spindle and slow-wave detectors, explicit control estimands, and multimodal measurements. Biomarker-guided and closed-loop acupuncture should presently be regarded as a research framework rather than an established treatment strategy.

item.title: Neuroimaging of Anxiety in Mild Cognitive Impairment: Integrating Structural, Functional, Molecular, and Network Perspectives-A Narrative Review.
item.description:
International journal of general medicine
This narrative review summarizes neuroimaging evidence on the neurobiological correlates of anxiety symptoms in mild cognitive impairment (MCI) across the Alzheimer's disease continuum. A literature search was conducted in PubMed from 1 January 2015 to 30 June 2026. Structural magnetic resonance imaging studies link anxiety to atrophy in medial temporal and prefrontal-limbic regions, with white matter disruption in the cingulum bundle and uncinate fasciculus. Functional magnetic resonance imaging shows altered interactions among the default mode network, salience network, and central executive network. Molecular imaging points to limbic glucose hypometabolism, amyloid deposition, and neuroinflammation. Emerging vascular and peripheral biomarker data further implicate blood-brain barrier disruption and gut-brain axis alterations. Most of the literature is cross-sectional and relies on heterogeneous anxiety assessments. Findings are further complicated by symptom overlap with depression and other neuropsychiatric manifestations, and anxiety-specific imaging studies in MCI are relatively scarce. Direct evidence specific to anxiety in MCI remains limited; some findings discussed here are derived from studies of Alzheimer's disease dementia or general neuropsychiatric symptoms and should be interpreted accordingly. Longitudinal multimodal designs, standardized anxiety-specific instruments, and integrative models linking symptom dimensions to imaging and fluid biomarkers are needed to disentangle whether anxiety in MCI represents an early marker of neurodegeneration, a disease-course modifier, or both.

item.title: Association Between Behavioral Activation System, White Matter Microstructure, and Depressive Symptoms in Major Depressive Disorder
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Reduced behavioral activation system (BAS) sensitivity is a core behavioral phenotype of anhedonia, a key symptom of major depressive disorder (MDD) that involves multifaceted dysfunctions in the reward processing system. However, the white matter microstructural basis of this phenotype remains unclear. We examined fractional anisotropy (FA) in 54 MDD patients and 72 healthy controls (HC) and explored relationships among FA, BAS Total scores, and depressive symptom severity (Beck Depression Inventory, BDI) in MDD patients. All participants underwent diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) and completed the BDI, BAS, and Behavioral Inhibition System (BIS) scales. Tract-based spatial statistics (TBSS) was used to extract FA values from seven a priori white matter tracts. Compared with HC, the MDD group showed significantly lower FA values in six tracts (right superior corona radiata, superior longitudinal fasciculus, posterior thalamic radiation, genu of corpus callosum, sagittal stratum, and fornix), as well as significantly lower BAS Total scores and higher BDI scores. Partial correlation analyses within the MDD group showed that FA values in four tracts (right superior corona radiata, superior longitudinal fasciculus, posterior thalamic radiation, and sagittal stratum) were significantly positively correlated with BAS Total scores. Mediation analyses controlling for age, sex, and BIS score revealed that BAS Total scores significantly mediated the relationship between FA values in these four tracts and BDI scores, with an indirect-only mediation pattern. When BIS was tested as an alternative mediator, none of the indirect effects were significant, supporting the specificity of the BAS-mediated pathway. These findings provide new imaging evidence for a "white matter microstructure–behavior–symptom" pathway, suggesting that targeting white matter microstructure and BAS function may help alleviate anhedonia in MDD.

item.title: Brain Structural Changes in Blast-Exposed Special Operations Forces Soldiers.
item.description:
Journal of neurotrauma
Special Operations Forces (SOF) soldiers experience frequent low-level occupational blast exposure and mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI), but the cumulative effects of these exposures on long-term neurological health remain poorly understood. The purpose of this longitudinal cohort study was to investigate associations between occupational blast exposure and brain structural change in SOF soldiers and to determine whether mTBI sustained between assessments moderated these associations. Male SOF soldiers (n = 88) underwent T1- and T2-weighted magnetic resonance imaging at two timepoints. Volumetric segmentation was performed using FreeSurfer. Main outcomes were percent change in global brain tissue volumes, including cerebral cortex, cerebral white matter, lateral ventricles, subcortical gray matter, and cerebellar cortex. Exposure was quantified as months between Time 1 and Time 2, used as a proxy for cumulative occupational blast exposure during time in a high-tempo operational unit. The number of self-reported mTBIs sustained between timepoints was categorized as 0, 1-2, or 3 or more injuries. The Benjamini-Hochberg procedure was applied to control the false discovery rate. Greater occupational blast exposure predicted increased lateral ventricle percent change (F 1,86 = 9.86; B = 0.126%; R 2 = 0.103; p = 0.002; p -adjusted = 0.012) and decreased cerebellar cortex percent change (F 1,86 = 5.72; B = -0.074%; R 2 = 0.062; p = 0.019; p -adjusted = 0.047). Between-visit mTBI did not significantly moderate these associations. In this cohort of SOF soldiers, greater cumulative occupational blast exposure was associated with lateral ventricular expansion and cerebellar cortex volume loss. The rate of ventricular expansion observed in this study is atypical compared with expected change in healthy adults and may represent an early structural marker of blast-related brain vulnerability. Cerebellar cortex volume loss may reflect regional susceptibility to blast-related injury. Identifying brain structural changes associated with occupational blast exposure may help inform exposure-monitoring strategies and targeted interventions to preserve warfighter brain health and readiness.

item.title: Multivariate Searchlight Decoding of Structural Disconnection and Network Features for Predicting Post-Stroke Deficits.
item.description:
Journal of neural engineering
Objective Lesion-symptom mapping and structural disconnection analyses have advanced our understanding of post-stroke deficits but remain predominantly based on forward inference, limiting identification of regions specifically predictive of behavioral impairment. We developed a multivariate voxelwise searchlight decoding framework for inverse inference integrating probabilistic structural disconnection with network-topological features. Approach. The analysis included 326 stroke patients from the GRECogVASC cohort assessed six months after stroke. For each patient, an age-specific probabilistic structural disconnection map was reconstructed using normative diffusion MRI tractography from 403 healthy controls. Within each voxel-centered searchlight, four features were extracted: disconnection probability, degree, clustering coefficient, and closeness centrality. Support vector machine classifiers were trained within deficit-specific decoding spaces using balanced bootstrap aggregation and majority voting to predict motor, executive, and processing-action-speed impairments. Statistical significance was assessed using 1,000 permutations, retaining voxels that consistently performed above chance across bootstrap iterations. Decoding-derived regions were subsequently assessed for within-cohort individual-level classification. Main results. Initial validation focused on left and right motor impairments, identifying predictive regions primarily within the contralateral precentral gyrus, internal capsule, and corticospinal tract, with mean accuracy ranges of 68.7-77.9%, 66.4-74.6%, and 64.8-71.8%, respectively. At the individual level, decoding-derived masks preserved overall classification performance, with accuracy improvements of up to 2.6% for individual deficits while reducing voxel dimensionality by up to 95.4%. Executive dysfunction and processing-action-speed deficits showed statistically above-chance but lower accuracies (54.5-66.9%). Executive dysfunction involved predominantly left-lateralized frontotemporal regions, whereas processing-action-speed deficits involved distributed fronto-insular, temporal, parietal, visual-association, and commissural pathways. Significance. The multivariate searchlight decoding framework integrating structural disconnection and network topology provides an inverse-inference approach complementary to lesion- and disconnection-symptom mapping for identifying spatially specific predictive patterns after stroke. The strong motor findings provide proof-of-concept support for the approach, whereas the cognitive results support its extension to distributed behavioral domains while underscoring the need for independent replication before neuroanatomical or clinical interpretation (Clinical trial registration: NCT01339195).

item.title: The anatomo-functional organization of the indirect pallido-subthalamic pathway in humans combining histology and diffusion imaging.
item.description:
NeuroImage
The subthalamic nucleus (STN) integrates cortical motor and emotional information with a posterior motor domain and an anterior limbic domain. However, the detailed anatomo-functional organisation of the STN in humans remains incomplete, largely because the indirect pathway linking the STN and the external globus pallidus (GPe) is difficult to image. Here, we characterize the GPe-STN pathway using histology combined with high-resolution diffusion imaging. We scanned three ex vivo specimens at 11.7 Tesla and ten healthy volunteers at 3 Tesla with ultra-high gradient. Brain sections were immunostained, reconstructed in 3D, and registered to define regions of interest in both datasets. Structural connectivity was assessed using probabilistic tractography (MRtrix), with homogeneously distributed seed points to maximize streamlines reconstruction. We found that GPe-STN streamlines follow fiber bundles that traverse or bypass the internal GP and the internal capsule, ex and in vivo. Ex vivo tractography revealed distinct projection patterns of limbic, associative, and sensorimotor GPe streamlines, targeting the anteromedial STN (24% volume coverage) and the posterocentral STN (67% and 30% coverage, respectively). In vivo tractography revealed a similar spatial organization, particularly in the right hemisphere, with consistent patterns across individuals. A substantial overlap was observed between associative and sensorimotor territories, whereas the limbic territory appeared more segregated. The data-driven clustering of the STN based on GPe-connectivity fingerprints confirms these findings. These results challenge the classical tripartite model of the basal ganglia and provide new insights into the STN anatomo-functional organization and support individualized targeting for functional neurosurgery.

item.title: Ultra-processed food intake during pregnancy and its association with early brain and behavioral development in children: a prospective cohort study.
item.description:
Reviews in endocrine & metabolic disorders
Growing evidence suggests that maternal consumption of ultra-processed foods (UPFs) during pregnancy may adversely affect offspring neurodevelopment. However, the underlying neurobiological mechanisms remain poorly understood. This study combines a comprehensive review of the current literature on maternal UPF consumption during pregnancy, brain development, and behavioral outcomes with empirical evidence from a prospective birth cohort. Specifically, we examined whether neonatal white matter (WM) microstructure may represent a pathway linking maternal UPF consumption with early behavioral development. Data were analyzed from three subsamples of mother-child pairs participating in the Barcelona Life Study Cohort (BiSC; 2018-2021): 560 pairs with maternal dietary and 18-month behavioral data, 43 with maternal dietary and neonatal WM tractography data, and 32 with complete dietary, neuroimaging, and behavioral assessments. Maternal UPF consumption was assessed during the second trimester using food-frequency questionnaires. Neonatal WM microstructure was examined at one month of age using diffusion tensor imaging and deterministic tractography. Behavioral outcomes at 18 months were assessed using the Child Behavior Checklist for Ages 1½-5 (CBCL 1½-5) and the Modified Checklist for Autism in Toddlers, Revised (M-CHAT-R). Associations among UPF exposure, WM measures, and behavioral outcomes were analyzed using regression models with permutation testing and hierarchical regression analyses to assess potential mediation. Higher maternal UPFs consumption, was associated with greater behavioural dysregulation at 18 months, including oppositional-defiant, attention, withdrawn, aggressive, and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD)-related problems. Maternal UPF consumption was associated with variations in WM microstructure in the superior longitudinal fasciculus, cingulum bundle and forceps minor. These variations were further associated with less favorable behavioral outcomes. Diffusivity measures in the right superior longitudinal fasciculus attenuated the association between maternal UPF consumption and oppositional-defiant problems. Findings from both the literature review and cohort analyses support an association between maternal UPF consumption and early behavioral outcomes. Neonatal WM microstructure may represent a potential neurobiological pathway linking maternal dietary habits and early behavioral development.

item.title: MRI Assessment of Baseline White Matter Microstructure and Its Relationship With the Onset and Trajectory of Cancer-Related Cognitive Impairment in Breast Cancer Patients.
item.description:
Journal of magnetic resonance imaging : JMRI
Background White matter microstructure may be affected by cancer and its treatment, yet its association with subsequent cancer-related cognitive impairment (CRCI) remains unclear. Purpose To investigate whether baseline white matter diffusion metrics are associated with the time to CRCI onset and longitudinal cognitive trajectories. Study type Prospective longitudinal study. Population A total of 230 female patients (49.4 ± 8.6 years) with histopathologically confirmed breast cancer (50 Stage II, 180 Stage III) with planned neoadjuvant chemotherapy before surgery. Field strength/sequence A 3 T, multi-shell SE-EPI DWI. Assessment Diffusion MRI was performed before chemotherapy (baseline). Neuropsychological assessments were carried out at baseline, after the first cycle of chemotherapy, after completion of chemotherapy but before surgery, and at 2-4 years after surgery. Diffusion tensor metrics (mean, radial, and axial diffusivity [MD, RD, and AD]), diffusion kurtosis metrics (axial and radial kurtosis [AK and RK]), and neurite orientation dispersion and density imaging metrics (orientation dispersion index [ODI], neurite density index [NDI]) were extracted from 25 white matter tracts, capturing both mean values and peak width. Statistical tests Cox regression and linear mixed-effects models assessed associations with time to CRCI onset and cognitive trajectories, respectively. A p value < 0.05 was considered significant. Results Higher ODI (anterior limb of the internal capsule [ALIC]: HR = 1.28), lower AD (ALIC: HR = 0.72, external capsule [EC]: HR = 0.73, superior fronto-occipital fasciculus [SFO]: HR = 0.70), and greater peak width of AK (ALIC: HR = 1.29, EC: HR = 1.24, genu of the corpus callosum [GCC]: HR = 1.32) were associated with earlier CRCI onset. Lower FA, RK, and MK (β = 0.13 to 0.27 × 10-3 ), higher MD, RD, ODI, and ISOVF (β = -0.23 to -0.13 × 10-3 ), and higher peak width metrics (β = -0.34 to -0.13 × 10-3 ) were associated with poorer longitudinal cognitive trajectories. Conclusions Pretreatment white matter microstructure may help identify patients at greater risk of CRCI and poorer cognitive trajectories. Level of evidence: 2 Technical efficacy Stage 3.
